title: A theory for detecting the Turing instability on static and temporal multiplex networks
abstract: The purpose of this work is to introduce and discuss a general framework for performing a linear instability analysis on multiplex networks, in the absence of inter-layer diffusion, with the specific motivation of detecting the Turing instability. The formalism itself is presented in full generality for $m$-unknowns, each of which arise as solutions of non-autonomous reaction-diffusion equations, on $n$-node temporal multiplex networks. In addition, we identify a class of multiplex networks for which the Laplacian matrices commute. In this setting analytical progress can be made and the explicit inequalities, governing instability, are derived. In order to explore our formalism we apply it to the specific example of a two-species predator-prey model on archipelagos. Here nodes are interpreted as islands and edges correspond to the transportation network for each species. Moreover, the non-autonomous setting is used to model a variety of natural phenomena.
summary: This paper introduces a general mathematical framework to analyze pattern formation (Turing instability) in coupled reaction-diffusion systems defined on multiplex networks. It extends standard stability analysis to handle time-varying and multi-layered network structures. The work is significant for its generality, providing tools to study complex ecological or chemical dynamics on realistic, interconnected systems.
main_problem: To develop a general framework for performing linear instability analysis, specifically detecting the Turing instability, on complex multiplex networks.
main_result: The framework successfully extends instability analysis to non-autonomous, multiplex networks, providing explicit criteria for instability when the network Laplacians commute.
method: The analysis involves linearizing the reaction-diffusion equations around a steady state and analyzing the eigenvalues of the resulting mode matrix, which is adapted for time-dependent and multiplex structures.
model_or_system: The study uses $m$-unknowns governed by non-autonomous reaction-diffusion equations on $n$-node temporal multiplex networks. An application is the two-species predator-prey model on archipelagos.
key_observables: Eigenvalues of the mode matrix (determining stability), and the time evolution of the mode amplitudes ($w_{\alpha,\ell}(t)$).
important_parameters: Diffusion coefficients ($d_\alpha$), reaction kinetics parameters ($h_\alpha(t)$), and the time dependence of the network connectivity.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the absence of inter-layer diffusion and that the network structure can be analyzed via linearization, though the general case requires numerical solutions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of species concentrations ($u_k, v_k$) for predator-prey models on 16-node networks, showing the transition from pattern formation to wave-like dynamics as time progresses.
paper_structure: The paper first reviews the general theory for linear instability on multiplex networks, deriving explicit criteria for the commuting Laplacian case. It then applies this theory to a predator-prey model, analyzing both static and time-dependent scenarios, culminating in numerical simulations.
why_interesting: While the core topic is reaction-diffusion dynamics, the mathematical tools developed for analyzing coupled, time-dependent systems on complex topologies (multiplex networks) are highly relevant to modeling open quantum systems or quantum information flow across interconnected quantum modules.
